notes.trap: Out-of-domain input does not return NULL or raise an error, even under ANSI mode. It returns NaN, which is not NULL, so `IS NULL` checks and `coalesce(...)` will not catch it.
Inputs below 1 silently return NaN rather than NULL or an error. NaN passes through `coalesce(...)` and IS NULL filters unchanged.
At the domain boundary, atanh(1) returns Infinity rather than an error or NULL. Values beyond the boundary return NaN.
cot(0) is computed as 1/tan(0) in floating point. It returns Infinity, not a divide-by-zero error or NULL.
Unlike `asin(...)` and similar functions that return NaN, Spark's logarithm functions return NULL for inputs <= 0. They do not return -Infinity, NaN, or an error.
Non-positive input returns NULL rather than NaN or an error. This can silently turn rows into NULLs.
Without a scale argument, ceiling of a DOUBLE returns BIGINT, not DOUBLE. With a scale argument, the result is DECIMAL instead.
NULL arguments are skipped, so the result is NULL only when every argument is NULL. Some engines (e.g. MySQL) instead return NULL if any argument is NULL.
A NULL seed is not an error and does not mean 'unseeded'. `random(null)` behaves exactly like `random(0)`, so it returns the same repeatable sequence.
`signum(...)` always returns DOUBLE (-1.0, 0.0 or 1.0), even for integer or interval input. Code that expects an INT sign value gets a double instead.
With ANSI mode off (the default), plain `-` on INT silently wraps around on overflow. `try_subtract(...)` returns NULL instead, so the two forms give different answers for the same inputs.
`tan(...)` is computed in floating point on an approximate pi. At pi/2 it returns a huge finite number rather than NULL, Infinity or an error.
`sinh(...)` overflows to the DOUBLE value Infinity rather than returning NULL or raising an error, even when ANSI mode is on.
